aiStories.title: 我不想读那些不是你写出来的文字
aiStories.originalTitle: I don't want to read what you didn't write
aiStories.fullContent:
People who rarely produced original writing are suddenly producing extensive design proposals, business plans, documentation, presentations, tickets, pull requests, blog articles, and meeting summaries, all generated by AI. It is all unreadable. AI is helping me write better and faster, but I’m fed up with reading almost anything written by AI. In this essay, I want to express my frustration, and describe how I’m finding value in AI for writing.

A pattern I see is that people use AI to build something new, then they use AI to retrospectively summarize what they have already built into a design document. Reading a document like this isn’t just difficult—it is punishing. The design document is no longer a proposal to build consensus, bring people along with you, and refine ideas through slow, deliberate thinking—it is a summary made by a machine, in exhausting detail, without context or perspective. It is unreadable. Inhumane. The authors of these documents become impatient when people aren’t engaged, and it is hard not to be, because the thing they built is already working.[1]

I also see more and more pull request summaries clearly written by machines for machines. They are rich in detail: this was changed to that, these things were split, those things were merged, this was left untouched, tests were added for this, and so on. But I’m left asking: Why are we doing this? What is the value? How risky or urgent is this work? Where do you want my input? What should I pay attention to? The same goes for tickets or meeting summaries made by AI. The writing, like more and more of the world, consists of statements outside of context.

I had someone write me a personal message about a sensitive topic that was clearly workshopped with AI in an effort to nuance the conversation and not offend me. But the message became impersonal, dispassionate, and disjointed. It had all of the parts, but it didn’t make sense as a whole. I wasn’t interested in reading it, or responding. I would much rather someone be themselves and write with their own voice, or with some passion, even if they can’t quite find the words, or risk offending me.

In relationships with others, there is vulnerability and risk. In communicating with your AI, there is none, and attempts to eliminate vulnerability and risk will eliminate the process of relationship itself. As Simon Sarris writes in Resist Summary, an essay I keep returning to:

I think one should write as much as they can with their own empiricism, their own senses, giving the reader their own characterization of life or events. —Simon Sarris, Resist Summary

Perhaps the laziest and most offensive use of AI writing I have seen: I had someone use AI to summarize my comments on their proposal as their response to me! Thanks! I couldn’t have said it better myself![2]

Cynthia Dunlop recently shared survey results on reading AI-written articles entitled Report: How developers react to AI-scented blog posts. For the majority of readers, if they think an article is AI-assisted or AI-authored, they will stop reading (78%) and avoid the author in the future (71%). As Bryan Cantrill wrote about this research in his essay The revolt of the reader: “our brains pull an LLM-triggered ejection handle, bailing us out mid-sentence in an act of self-preservation.”

The strongest result in the survey was people overwhelmingly preferred the author’s own writing (98%), with all its flaws and idiosyncrasies, as compared to a soulless rewrite by an AI. Writing authentically is one of the best ways to connect with people. It reminds me of a comment Bjarne Stroustrup, the creator of C++, made during a panel discussion I attended over a decade ago on writing books:

When I read a book, I really feel that if I can hear the author’s voice ringing in my head—complete with weird accents and peculiarities of their speaking patterns—then I feel like something has succeeded. If it feels like dry, academic text, somebody has written yet another dry, academic text. And so, giving talks about the subject really helps. And, for many people, ... I can hear them when I read it, and that is good. —Bjarne Stroustrup[3]

When you are the one who prompted the AI, the written output is often quite useful. But do not mistake this for effective writing. When you read the output, you already have lots of context—you formulated the prompts, established the constraints, and provided artefacts like documentation, source code, logs, statistics, pictures, etc., that led to the output. You can skim the output and quickly decide what is relevant and valuable versus what is irrelevant or wrong. You are also part of the process—prompting the AI and seeing the results—a call and an answer. You bring a human perspective to the machine. When you send the same text to someone else, they have little to no context. They are not part of the process—there is no unfolding—so it is much harder to decide what is relevant versus what is not. They are forced to read exhaustively and consider every line, peering into the internals of a machine with the hope of establishing context. It is only natural to stop reading.

I recently wrote an academic paper.[4] I used AI extensively and it made the writing process faster and more enjoyable. But AI did not write a single line of the paper. I wrote the paper in LaTeX. The context I provided to the AI included the journal style guide and LaTeX template, all papers previously published in the journal, the source code for the software systems I was writing about, and the configuration, logs, and metrics for production deployments of the software.

After writing a paragraph, many times I would ask the AI to ensure what I had written was correct by referencing the source code or configuration, or examining production logs or metrics. For example, ensuring I had correctly described which columns in the database were indexed, or how the rows in the Parquet files were sorted. This allowed me to stay in the context of writing, often moving on to the next paragraph while the AI verified the previous one. It helped me spot important omissions and inaccuracies. Remarkably, reversing this process—asking the AI to write the paragraph from the context I provided, like describing how something works from the source code—was never valuable. Not once. It was consistently unpleasant to read, and often inaccurate.

Another thing that helped me stay in context was using AI to complete the citations. It is tedious to look up the details of a paper, website, or book, fill in the BibTeX format, and then reference it in the text. Instead, I would leave parenthetic instructions for the AI to reference what I wanted, and then keep on writing without breaking stride.[5]

The AI was incredibly good—indeed ruthless—at finding spelling and grammar mistakes. It was great at suggesting simplifications to sentences that are too long or unclear.[6] It was skilled at drawing technical diagrams in TikZ, again speeding up the work, and saving me from learning this syntax. The AI even found a very subtle mistake where I had used the incorrect notation in one paragraph, something four human reviewers who were experts in the system all missed.[7]

What was the one thing the AI was incredibly good at writing? It wrote the abstract—the most terse, mechanical, inhuman part of the whole paper—indeed, the most abstracted part. I included it entirely unchanged. Perhaps this shouldn’t be a surprise, as AI is great at summary, abstraction, and re-presentation of original work.

It would be a mistake to underestimate the writing that can one day be achieved by AI. We are still in the very early days of model development, and the models most of us are using are trained to be factual, direct, and correct, rather than creative. However, Murat Demirbas’s excellent essay The Safest Job from AI may be Writing notes that the quality of writing from LLMs has plateaued and it may be difficult to improve since unlike programming, mathematics, and accounting, it is difficult to provide a clear formulation and verifiable output.[8]

Since LLMs lack an active mental model of a specific human reader, they are just optimizing for the statistical probability of the next word over a vast dataset. They cannot empathize with the human reader, as they don’t have the human lived experience. And they have zero skin in the game. —Murat Demirbas, The Safest Job from AI may be Writing

I am interested in two efforts to improve AI writing that I’ve recently come across. The first is ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, a standard for writing technical documentation that grew out of an aerospace working group in the 1980s. It has two parts: a controlled dictionary and writing rules about grammar and style. A version of ASD-STE100 has been created for use with AI models.[9] ASD-STE100 isn’t appropriate for all AI-generated writing—it is specifically targeted at clear and easy-to-follow instruction manuals. I’m going to give it a try for installation instructions, runbooks, and similar documentation.

The second is Pangram, a model fine-tuned to detect AI writing. Bryan Cantrill in the essay The revolt of the reader notes:

To use an LLM to write is to void the social contract between writer and reader: we readers shouldn’t be expected to labor to understand a sentence that the writer themselves didn’t work to create. —Bryan Cantrill, The revolt of the reader

I could not agree more. Bryan has started experimenting with Pangram to detect AI-generated writing that violates this contract and has gone so far as to mandate that all public writing at Oxide be reported by Pangram as human-authored. A tool like this could save us from the laziest and worst AI writing.[10]

When we write, the meaning of our words is not always direct, factual, or concise. Examples include poetry, literature, song, mythology, humour, and theatre. Iain McGilchrist, who I believe is one of the most important writers of our generation, writes in the book The Matter with Things: “The more important something is, the more we have to struggle in the attempt to reduce it to language.” Ask an LLM what the reliable formula is for falling in love. In AI-generated writing, detailed information gives the illusion of meaning. But in mimicking human knowledge, intelligence, and understanding, an AI writing about the facts is very different from the quality of writing from a lived experience. The whole cannot be decomposed into parts without a substantial loss of meaning.

The direct approach destroys its object. Similarly, there are things that can be conveyed only indirectly. To recapture the depth of what is said, or in order to say anything truly new, we are always engaged in going beyond everyday language, which means being alert to what is being said implicitly. —Iain McGilchrist, The Matter with Things

It might seem silly to say that writing in business, engineering, or science should involve uncertainty, not just facts and conclusions. But operations, incident response, product development, performance engineering, hunting for security vulnerabilities, performance reviews, mission statements, and many other endeavours, are all creative and involve uncertainty. The narrative is regularly as important as the facts and conclusions. It is also easy to anthropomorphize LLMs as good systems thinkers because they can synthesize such a wide range of information. However, returning to Simon Sarris: “narrative resists compression” and “the opposite of summary is attention to detail”.

Despite an emphasis on linear, first-principles thinking, the work of a good systems engineer, just like the work of a good anthropologist or psychologist, is difficult to put into words, and especially into summary. You can’t necessarily observe and write things down using a formula. Even writing things down loses some of the context. The observer is also part of that context. Systems work always has some sense of discovery, holding open the unknown, an unfolding of relationship with the system itself, and a willingness to be surprised. Normal language doesn’t always have the words.[11]

The nature of the output, of summary, is speed things along. But the consequence is to avoid you having to build your own complex mental model of anything. I worry that without a complex model in one’s own mind, one may never notice complex relationships that are otherwise missed. A loss of attention to detail. —Simon Sarris, Resist Summary

I don’t want to live in a world where you use AI to summarize something important into unreadable text, and then I use AI in an attempt to decipher it. I want to hear you, imperfections and all. I want your interpretation of aesthetics, beauty, quality, relationship, time. I want to know how you feel. I want you to cut through and tell me what really matters. I don’t want to read a summary of facts and connections separate from experience and relationship. As Iain McGilchrist describes, the way we attend to the world changes the nature of what comes into being, the only world we can know.[12]

If you ask a machine to do something for you, you are at risk of not asking for what you want, but what it can do well. If what it can do well is summarize, and you rely upon the tool, you may tune your questions so that you get better answers. This looks like training a machine to do what you want, but its also training yourself to ask questions about the world in a certain way. What are the questions you are omitting? —Simon Sarris, Resist Summary

Intentional writing will likely become more valuable. People who write, and write to think, to think deeply and carefully, or to create, to share, or to capture something important without explicitly expressing it will continue to write and produce original work. The people who never were writers will use AI to produce lots of text.

In some instances, design documents are not the right fit, and using AI to rapidly collaborate around working software is perhaps a better approach to refine ideas and build consensus. ↩︎

In another example, a group of people had been working on a proposal, building consensus through a number of wiki pages. Someone new wanted to modify the proposal. Rather than going through the messy, relational process of working with this group to update the existing wiki pages, they used AI to proliferate a new wiki page, copying the existing work and adding their own twist. ↩︎

I’ve used this quote previously in Techniques for Improving Your Technical Writing. ↩︎

The paper describes a database I created and my hope is it will be accepted to The Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR). ↩︎

For example, I would write: {TODO: reference the Amazon Aurora paper} and the AI would take care of the rest. ↩︎

I also use AI as an editor for my blog. It gives me more confidence posting an essay without having someone else proofread it. But I only let AI identify errors or make suggestions. I don’t let it rewrite and change my voice or perspective. ↩︎

I was describing a log-structured merge (LSM). We had originally called the levels Generation 1, Generation 2, Generation 3, or Gen1, Gen2, Gen3 for short. In the paper, I described the LSM more generically using L0, L1, L2 for Level 0, Level 1, Level 2, respectively. This meant my colleagues reading this paper had to map L1 to Gen2 in their heads, which made my error in one paragraph of incorrectly using L1 when I meant L2 extra hard to spot. The LLM found it, no problem. ↩︎

Another interesting essay on the limitations of AI for writing, especially the individuality in understanding, is The Human Skill That Eludes AI: Why can’t language models write well? by Jasmine Sun in The Atlantic. ↩︎

Thanks to Chris Riccomini for making me aware of this. ↩︎

For more on Pangram, listen to the Oxide and Friends podcast with the founder Max Spero. One thing they note is there is some evidence that people who use LLMs regularly are good at detecting LLM writing, but people who do not are less adept. There is also an interesting discussion about trying to reverse the prompt and the input context in an effort to describe how much of the output came from the input and how much came from the model. ↩︎

The best systems thinkers I know tend to be excellent writers. I expect this skill to remain important and perhaps become even more important. Returning to Murat Demirbas’s essay on writing that I referenced earlier, it concludes: “And maybe programming itself is turning into a form of creative writing, getting more opinionated and more architectural.” ↩︎

Iain also draws the distinction between comprehension—taking the world as a whole—and apprehension—taking hold of the world. The quality of attention is different. I find it interesting that while apprehension is the act of seizing or capturing, it is also a fearful or uneasy anticipation of the future. I highly recommend watching Iain’s lecture AI and the Battle for the Soul: Information is Not Understanding at Ralston College. ↩︎
aiStories.fullTranslation:
那些过去鲜少原创写作的人，突然之间开始大量产出详尽的设计方案、商业计划书、技术文档、演示文稿、工单、代码拉取请求（PR）、博客文章和会议纪要——而所有这些都是由 AI 生成的。这一切根本让人读不下去。AI 确实在帮我写得更好、更快，但我已经受够了去读几乎任何由 AI 撰写的东西。在这篇文章中，我想表达我的沮丧，并分享我是如何在写作中发现 AI 的真正价值的。

我观察到的一种模式是：人们使用 AI 构建出某种新事物，然后又使用 AI 事后总结他们已经构建好的内容，并拼凑成一份设计文档。阅读这样的文档不仅令人痛苦，简直是一种折磨。这份设计文档不再是一个用来凝聚共识、带领他人理解思路、并通过缓慢深思熟虑来打磨观点的提案——而变成了一台机器以令人精疲力竭的细节所做出的总结，毫无语境，也没有任何思考视角。它味同嚼蜡，毫无温度。当人们提不起兴趣阅读时，这些文档的作者还会变得不耐烦，而读者很难不感到乏味，毕竟作者做出来的东西已经在运行了。[1]

我还看到越来越多显然是“机器写给机器看”的 PR 总结。它们细节丰富：这里改成了那里，这些内容被拆分，那些内容被合并，这部分保持不变，为这部分添加了测试用例，等等。但我心中始终存在疑问：我们为什么要这么做？它的价值是什么？这项工作的风险或紧急程度如何？你希望我在哪里提出建议？我应该重点关注什么？由 AI 生成的工单或会议纪要也是如此。就像世界上越来越多的内容一样，这些文字由脱离语境的孤立陈述堆砌而成。

曾有人就一个敏感话题给我发来一条私信，字里行间明显经过了 AI 的反复润色，试图让措辞更显微妙、避免冒犯我。但这条信息却变得毫无个性、缺乏情感且支离破碎。它具备了所有该有的要素，但整篇读下来却不知所云。我毫无兴趣去读，也懒得回复。我宁愿对方做真实的自己，用自己的声音或带着某种情感来写，哪怕他们找不到最恰当的措辞，或者冒着可能冒犯我的风险。

在与他人的交往中，脆弱与风险是必然存在的。而在与 AI 沟通时，则完全没有这些；试图消除脆弱与风险的做法，最终会消解人际交往过程本身。正如西蒙·萨里斯（Simon Sarris）在我经常重温的文章《抵制总结》（Resist Summary）中所写：
“我认为，人应该尽可能凭借自己的经验、自己的感官去写作，向读者展现自己对生活或事件的独特描摹。”——西蒙·萨里斯，《抵制总结》

我见过的也许最懒惰、最无礼的 AI 写作用法是：有人居然用 AI 总结了我对其提案的批注，并将这份总结作为给我的回复！真是多谢了！我自己说得都没这么好！[2]

辛西娅·邓洛普（Cynthia Dunlop）最近分享了一份关于阅读 AI 撰写文章的调查结果，题为《报告：开发者如何看待带有“AI 味”的博客文章》（Report: How developers react to AI-scented blog posts）。对于绝大多数读者而言，如果他们认为一篇文章是 AI 辅助或由 AI 生成的，78% 的人会停止阅读，71% 的人未来会避开该作者。正如布莱恩·坎特里尔（Bryan Cantrill）在其文章《读者的反抗》（The revolt of the reader）中针对该研究所写的那样：“我们的大脑会拉动由大语言模型触发的弹射手柄，为了自我保护而半句弃读。”

该调查中最显著的结果是，与 AI 毫无灵魂的改写相比，人们压倒性地倾向于作者亲笔写下的文字（98%），哪怕其中带着种种瑕疵和怪癖。真诚地写作是与他人建立联结的最佳方式之一。这让我想起十多年前我参加的一个关于写书的小组讨论中，C++ 创始人本贾尼·斯特劳斯特卢普（Bjarne Stroustrup）所做的一番评论：
“当我读一本书时，如果我真切地能在脑海中听到作者的声音在回响——伴随着奇怪的口音和他们独特的说话模式——那么我就觉得这本书成功了。如果感觉像是枯燥的学术文本，那无非就是有人写了又一篇枯燥的学术文本而已。因此，围绕该主题做演讲真的很有帮助。对于许多人来说……我在阅读时能听见他们的声音，这很好。”——本贾尼·斯特劳斯特卢普[3]

当你作为给 AI 提供提示词的人时，生成的文字往往非常有用。但切勿将其误以为是高效的写作。当你阅读这些生成的内容时，你脑海中已经有了大量语境——是你构思了提示词、设定了限制条件，并提供了生成输出所需的文档、源代码、日志、统计数据、图片等素材。你可以快速浏览输出结果，并迅速判断出哪些内容相关且有价值，哪些内容无关或错误。你本身也是这个过程的一部分——向 AI 提问并查看结果——这是一问一答的交互。是你为机器赋予了人类的视角。然而，当你把同样的文本发送给别人时，他们几乎没有任何背景信息。他们并没有参与这个生成过程——缺乏思维展开的脉络——因此要判断哪些内容相关、哪些不相关就会困难得多。他们被迫逐字逐句阅读并思考每一行，试图窥探机器内部以建立语境。在这种情况下，中途放弃阅读再自然不过了。

我最近写了一篇学术论文。[4] 我大量使用了 AI，它让写作过程更快、更愉快。但论文中没有一句话是 AI 代笔的。我是用 LaTeX 撰写这篇论文的。我提供给 AI 的上下文包括期刊的排版指南和 LaTeX 模板、该期刊此前发表过的所有论文、我所撰写的软件系统的源代码，以及该软件生产环境部署的配置、日志和指标。

每写完一个段落，我常常会要求 AI 参考源代码或配置，或者检查生产日志或指标，以核实我所写的内容是否正确。例如，确认我是否准确描述了数据库中哪些列建立了索引，或者 Parquet 文件中的行是如何排序的。这使我能够完全沉浸在写作状态中，经常是在 AI 验证上一段的同时，我已经开始写下一段。它帮助我发现了重要的疏漏和不准确之处。值得注意的是，如果将这个过程反过来——让 AI 根据我提供的上下文来编写段落，比如根据源代码描述某些功能是如何运作的——则从来没有产生过任何价值。一次都没有。生成出来的东西读起来始终令人不适，而且往往漏洞百出。

另一项帮助我保持专注的做法是使用 AI 来补全参考文献引用。查找论文、网站或书籍的详细信息，填写 BibTeX 格式，然后在正文中进行引用，是一件非常繁琐的事。与其如此，我会在括号中留下指令，让 AI 去引用我想要的内容，从而保持写作思路不被打断。[5]

人工智能在挑出拼写和语法错误方面表现得异乎寻常地好——甚至可以说是毫不留情。它非常擅长对过长或不够清晰的句子提出简化建议。[6] 它还精通使用 TikZ 绘制技术图表，这再次加快了工作进度，让我免于学习这种语法的负担。AI 甚至在一个段落中发现了我使用错误记号的一个极其微小的失误，而四位作为该系统专家的评审人类专家全都漏掉了这一点。[7]

AI 究竟有一项什么任务写得格外好？它撰写了论文摘要——这是整篇论文中最简练、最机械、最缺乏人性的一部分——确实也是最“抽象”（abstracted）的部分。我一字未改地直接采用了它。或许这并不令人意外，因为 AI 本就极擅长总结、抽象以及对原始工作进行重新表述。

低估 AI 未来某一天所能达到的写作水平将是一个错误。我们目前仍处于模型发展的非常早期阶段，而且我们大多数人正在使用的模型被训练得注重事实、直接且准确，而非注重创造力。然而，穆拉特·德米尔巴斯（Murat Demirbas）在其优秀随笔《AI 面前最安全的工作或许是写作》中指出，大语言模型（LLM）的写作质量已经进入平台期，且可能难以进一步提升，因为与编程、数学和会计不同，写作很难提供清晰的形式化表述和可验证的输出结果。[8]

“由于 LLM 缺乏针对特定人类读者的主动心智模型，它们仅仅是在庞大的数据集上对下一个词的统计概率进行优化。它们无法与人类读者产生共鸣，因为它们没有人类的真实生活体验。而且它们在这场游戏中毫无切身利益（zero skin in the game）。”——穆拉特·德米尔巴斯，《AI 面前最安全的工作或许是写作》

我最近接触到了两项旨在改善 AI 写作的尝试，对此我颇感兴趣。第一项是 ASD-STE100 简化技术英语（Simplified Technical English），这是 20 世纪 80 年代源于一个航空航天工作组的技术文档编写标准。它由两部分组成：一个受控词典以及关于语法和风格的写作规则。目前已有人针对 AI 模型开发了 ASD-STE100 的相应版本。[9] ASD-STE100 并不适用于所有 AI 生成的写作——它专门针对清晰且易于遵循的操作手册。我打算在安装指南、运维手册（runbooks）及类似文档中尝试使用它。

第二项是 Pangram，一个经过微调专门用于检测 AI 写作的模型。布莱恩·坎特里尔（Bryan Cantrill）在随笔《读者的反抗》中写道：

“使用 LLM 进行写作，就是撕毁了作者与读者之间的社会契约：我们作为读者，不应该被期望去费力理解一句作者自己都不曾费心创造的句子。”——布莱恩·坎特里尔，《读者的反抗》

我对此赞同得不能更多。布莱恩已经开始尝试使用 Pangram 来检测违反这一契约的 AI 生成文本，甚至已经严格规定 Oxide 公司的所有对外公开文字都必须被 Pangram 判定为由人类创作。像这样的工具或许能将我们从最懒惰、最拙劣的 AI 写作中拯救出来。[10]

当我们写作时，字里行间的意义并不总是直白、客观或精炼的。诗歌、文学、歌曲、神话、幽默和戏剧皆是例证。我认为是我们这一代最重要的作家之一的伊恩·麦吉尔克里斯特（Iain McGilchrist）在《事物的本质》（The Matter with Things）一书中写道：“一件事情越重要，我们在试图将其还原为语言时就越是艰难挣扎。”不妨去问问 LLM，坠入爱河的可靠公式是什么。在 AI 生成的写作中，详尽的细节信息制造了一种意义的幻象。但在模仿人类知识、智慧和理解的过程中，AI 针对事实所做的写作，与源于亲身经历的写作质量有着天壤之别。整体无法在不严重丧失意义的前提下被拆解为局部。

“直接切入的方法会毁掉其对象。同样，有些东西只能被间接传达。为了重新捕捉言语的深意，或者为了说出任何真正崭新的东西，我们始终在致力于超越日常语言，这意味着要对言外之意保持敏锐。”——伊恩·麦吉尔克里斯特，《事物的本质》

如果说商业、工程或科学领域的写作也应该包含不确定性，而不仅仅是事实与结论，这看似有些荒谬。但运维、事故响应、产品开发、性能工程、排查安全漏洞、绩效评估、使命陈述以及许多其他努力，全都具有创造性并伴随着不确定性。叙事往往与事实和结论同样重要。人们也很容易将 LLM 拟人化，认为它们是优秀的系统思考者，因为它们能综合如此广泛的信息。然而，正如西蒙·萨里斯（Simon Sarris）所言：“叙事抗拒压缩”，“总结的反面是对细节的关注”。

尽管人们强调线性与第一性原理思维，但一位优秀的系统工程师的工作，正如一位优秀的人类学家或心理学家的工作一样，很难用语言来表达，尤其难以化为总结。你未必能用某种公式来观察并记录事物。哪怕仅仅是将事情写下来，也会丢失部分语境。观察者本身就是该语境的一部分。系统性工作总是带有一种探索感、对未知的包容、与系统本身关系的展开，以及乐于接受意外的意愿。常规的语言并不总能找到恰当的词汇。[11]

“输出与总结的本质，在于加快进展速度。但其后果是让你避免在自己的头脑中构建针对任何事物的复杂心智模型。我担心，如果一个人自己的脑海中没有一个复杂的模型，他可能永远无法察觉到那些本会被遗漏的复杂关系。这是一种对细节关注的丧失。”——西蒙·萨里斯，《抗拒总结》（Resist Summary）

我不想生活在这样一个世界里：你用 AI 将重要的事物总结成难以卒读的文本，然后我又用 AI 试图去破译它。我想倾听你的声音，包括所有的不完美。我想要你对美学、美丽、品质、关系、时间的解读。我想知道你的感受。我希望你拨开迷雾，告诉我究竟什么才是真正重要的。我不想阅读脱离了经历与关系的所谓事实与关联的总结。正如伊恩·麦吉尔克里斯特所描述的那样，我们关注世界的方式，改变了正在生成的现实的本质，而那是我们所能知晓的唯一世界。[12]

“如果你要求机器为你做某事，你所面临的风险不是你没能要求你想要的东西，而是你只要求了它擅长做的事情。如果它擅长做的是总结，而你依赖于这个工具，你可能会调整你的提问方式以便获得更好的答案。这看起来是在训练机器按你的意图行事，但它同时也是在训练你自己以某种特定的方式向世界提问。那些被你忽略的问题又是什么呢？”——西蒙·萨里斯，《抗拒总结》

有意识的写作可能会变得更加珍贵。那些为了写作而写作、为了深入细致地思考而写作，或者为了创造、分享，亦或是为了捕捉某些重要事物而不直白表达出来的人，将继续写作并产出原创作品。而那些从未真正成为作者的人，则会利用人工智能生成海量文本。

在某些情况下，设计文档并不是最合适的工具，此时利用人工智能围绕可运行的软件迅速展开协作，或许是完善想法并凝聚共识的更好方法。↩︎

在另一个例子中，一群人一直在共同撰写一份提案，通过若干 Wiki 页面逐步建立共识。一位新加入的成员想要修改该提案。但他并没有经历与该团队共同更新现有 Wiki 页面那一复杂而关乎人际协作的过程，而是使用人工智能快速生成了一个新的 Wiki 页面，照搬了现有工作并添加了自己的想法。↩︎

我此前曾在《提升技术写作水平的技巧》（Techniques for Improving Your Technical Writing）中引用过这句话。↩︎

这篇论文介绍了我开发的一个数据库，我希望它能被创新数据系统研究研讨会（CIDR）接收。↩︎

例如，我会写下：{待办：引用 Amazon Aurora 论文}，剩下的交给人工智能处理就行。↩︎

我也将人工智能用作自己博客的编辑。这让我即使在没有他人帮忙校对的情况下，也能更有信心地发布文章。但我只让人工智能查找错误或提出建议，绝不会让它重写文章，以免改变我的语调或视角。↩︎

我当时在描述一种日志结构合并树（LSM）。我们最初将各层级称为 Generation 1、Generation 2、Generation 3，简称为 Gen1、Gen2、Gen3。在论文中，我使用了更通用的描述方式，分别用 L0、L1、L2 代表 Level 0、Level 1、Level 2。这意味着我的同事在阅读这篇论文时，必须在脑海中将 L1 映射为 Gen2，这使得我在某一段落中把本应写作 L2 的地方误写成 L1 的错误极难被发现。而大语言模型毫无障碍地指出了这个错误。↩︎

关于人工智能在写作方面的局限性——尤其是理解层面上的个体特异性，另一篇引人深思的文章是 Jasmine Sun 在《大西洋月刊》（The Atlantic）上发表的《逃脱人工智能的人类技能：为什么语言模型写不好文章？》（The Human Skill That Eludes AI: Why can’t language models write well?）。↩︎

感谢 Chris Riccomini 让我注意到这一点。↩︎

若想了解更多关于 Pangram 的信息，可以收听创始人 Max Spero 参与的 Oxide and Friends 播客。他们指出的一个现象是，有迹象表明经常使用大语言模型的人更擅长识别大模型生成的文字，而不常使用的人则较不擅长。此外，关于尝试对提示词和输入上下文进行逆向工程以分析输出内容中有多少源自输入、有多少源自模型的讨论也非常有趣。↩︎

我所认识的优秀系统思考者往往也是杰出的写作者。我认为这项技能将保持其重要性，甚至可能变得更加关键。回到我之前引用的 Murat Demirbas 讨论写作的文章，它的结语是：“或许编程本身正在演变成一种创意写作形式，变得越来越具主见，也越来越具架构性。”↩︎

伊恩（Iain）还区分了“全面领悟”（comprehension，即将世界视为一个整体）与“掌握捕获”（apprehension，即把持控制世界）。这两者所倾注的注意力本质不同。我觉得很有意思的是，虽然 apprehension 意味着抓取或捕获的行为，但它同时也代表着对未来的担忧或不安预期。我极力推荐观看伊恩在罗尔斯顿学院（Ralston College）的演讲《人工智能与灵魂之争：信息并非理解》（AI and the Battle for the Soul: Information is Not Understanding）。↩︎

aiStories.title: 如何评估 AI Agent：从工具调用到任务完成
aiStories.originalTitle: How to Evaluate AI Agents From Tool Calls to Task Completion
aiStories.source: NVIDIA Developer Blog (英伟达开发者官方英文)

aiStories.fullContent:
When you ship an AI agent, the key question is whether it can execute a chain of work across dozens of sequential tool calls against a live environment, and recover when a step fails. Scoring whether the model sounds right tells you almost nothing about whether the work finished.

That gap is why agent evaluation has had to evolve from scoring a single function call to scoring an entire task, with tool calling as the connective tissue underneath. This post traces that arc and explains why nearly every serious agent benchmark now rests on tool use.

The original harnesses were built for static tasks. The first model-agnostic, open-source harness decoupled the model from the evaluation protocol.

Agents broke this assumption. Operating across multi-step tasks, an agent calls tools, handles errors, and observes results over many steps, making a single output string insufficient. The Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) emerged to evaluate function selection and argument accuracy across single- and multi-turn scenarios. However, BFCL only evaluates individual calls—a valid issue_refund call still fails if underlying checks or updates were skipped. Call accuracy is necessary, but not sufficient.

Full agentic evaluation now requires a full execution environment: one that executes each tool call, tracks state across steps, and reads the world afterward to decide whether the work got done.

Two scoring layers sit on top of it:

Step-level tells you where the chain breaks, which is what you want when debugging or targeting fine-tuning effort; E2E collapses a failure on step one and a failure on step nine into the same “task failed.” E2E is what your users actually experience, which is why most production evals gate the release on it and keep step-level tracing underneath for debugging.

Those two scores are two readings of one object: the trace. A trace is the ordered log of a single attempt: the user message, each step, and the environment state when the attempt stops. Process scoring grades the rows. E2E scoring grades the final state.

A tool-calling benchmark scores three things in order: deciding to use a tool, selecting the right one, and populating its arguments. A model that reaches for a tool when a direct answer would fail as surely as one that skips a tool it needed. Cost and latency ride on top, set by the call’s verbosity and runtime.

Every run rolls up through a fixed hierarchy: Benchmark → Trial → Task → Turn → Step:

A step is usually a tool call, and every score above it rolls up from those steps. The metrics worth tracking collapse onto three axes: accuracy, verbosity, cost (see Table 1, below).

The pairings matter: success rate without consistency is a point estimate on a stochastic system (a model that hits 90% then 74% is a worse bet than one holding 84%); tool-call precision without argument accuracy hides slot-filling failures.

Step count is often the axis that varies most across models on the same task — four steps versus fifteen — though on suites like Terminal-Bench 2.0 steps-per-turn varies too, so which axis moves most is benchmark-dependent. Parallel tool calling cuts step count and latency, but not call count: a one-step turn firing four tools still issued four calls. Roll up in order; don’t average steps and call it a benchmark score.

Two benchmarks can both claim to test tool calling and produce numbers that aren’t comparable. Three dimensions explain most of the gap:

Contamination now extends beyond training data leaks to live variants: web-searching agents retrieving answer keys during evaluation, and datasets on Hugging Face quickly re-scraped into pretraining corpora. Private domain evals solve this by being unable to scrape.

Table 2, below, is a public trace from a real benchmark run using step-level and E2E scoring, where the suite rather than an artificial ticket provides the tools, user, and completion criteria.

Looking at the results that were outputted, it is important to look at the last 5 bullets: E2E check, E2E score, step level score, tool-call precision, and argument accuracy. E2E check tells us that the related tests for the bug issues it sought to fix passed, meaning E2E score in this case is 1 (is_resolved: true). The next metric is the step level score that tells you how many of the steps the model took were actually needed. Looking at the score for the table above, step level is 3/4 due to one of the steps in this case being redundant – in particular step 2. In this case, it directly plays into the tool-call precision which also received a 3/4 due to the minor misstep. For this trace, our final metric argument accuracy saw that all arguments filled in correctly with no malformed arguments.

The line between “calling a tool” and “completing a task” no longer holds: most benchmarks measuring general capability now also measure tool use because models aren’t run without tools in any viable deployment. A benchmark that withholds tool access scores a capability nobody ships.

Not every benchmark makes the case. HumanEval runs generated Python against unit tests, providing executable verification, but no tool call and no environment to act on. SWE-bench is where the shift becomes clear: resolving a real GitHub issue means navigating a codebase, writing a patch, and passing the suite — file-read, search, and edit calls in sequence. The score measures the outcome, but the trajectory underneath consists entirely of tool calls. In many cases, then, the benchmarks you already run for general capability are already exercising tool use. That reframes the question that matters:

Academic benchmarks measure a model’s capability ceiling in the abstract. Enterprise benchmarks answer the narrower, more useful question: can it do my job — your tasks, against your APIs, under your policies? The closer a benchmark sits to production, the more its score should weigh in your decision.

Read NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning’s published suite as task completion and time-to-done, not isolated call accuracy. Banking scores completion across a multi-turn banking conversation — the refund trace at scale, not a single call. GDPval-AA v2 scores real agentic work from actual job outputs, judged pairwise by a panel of LLM judges with Elo anchored to a 1,000 human-expert baseline — the kind of human validation that keeps a judge score trustworthy. On PinchBench, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning hits 86% accuracy while finishing 10,000 tasks 30% faster than Qwen3.6 35B at comparable accuracy — a model that finishes efficiently beats one scoring higher on isolated accuracy while burning more steps and tokens.

Public scores are a great signal, but they shouldn’t be considered as a release gate. Adapting the model to your task and use-cases is as important as ever.

Verify consequences in the environment, use judges for language, and use tool-call precision and argument accuracy to find where the chain breaks.

To reproduce the published numbers, Nemotron ships reproducibility docs covering the configs behind the model card scores. Try it on build.nvidia.com, grab weights from Hugging Face, or follow the NIM guide.

Tool calling in the realm of LLM benchmarking is the foundation that evaluations today rest on. Being able to build, read, and understand these evaluations is pertinent in making an informed decision for your use case.

Stay up to date on NVIDIA Nemotron by subscribing to NVIDIA news and following NVIDIA AI on LinkedIn, X, YouTube, and the Nemotron channel on Discord.

Access open Nemotron Models on Hugging Face and a collection of NIM microservices and Developer Examples on build.nvidia.com.
aiStories.fullTranslation:
当你发布一款 AI Agent（智能体）时，核心问题在于它能否在真实环境中跨越数十次连续的工具调用来执行工作链路，并在某一步骤失败时实现恢复。仅评估模型的回答听起来是否合理，几乎无法说明任务是否真正完成。

这种差距正是 Agent 评估不得不从单纯评估单次函数调用演进到评估整个任务的原因所在，而工具调用则是底层的连接纽带。本文将梳理这一演进脉络，并解释为何如今几乎所有严谨的 Agent 基准测试都建立在工具使用之上。

最初的测试框架是为静态任务构建的。首个与模型无关的开源测试框架将模型与评估协议解耦开来。

Agent 打破了这一假设。在跨越多步骤的任务中运行时，Agent 会调用工具、处理错误，并在多个步骤中观察结果，这使得单一的输出字符串不再足以作为评判标准。伯克利函数调用排行榜（BFCL）应运而生，用于评估单轮和多轮场景下的函数选择与参数准确性。然而，BFCL 仅评估单个调用——如果底层的检查或更新被跳过，一次合法的 issue_refund 调用实际上依然是失败的。调用的准确性是必要的，但并不充分。

如今，完整的 Agent 化评估需要一个完整的执行环境：该环境能够执行每次工具调用、跨步骤跟踪状态，并在事后读取现实环境状态以判定工作是否真正完成。

在其之上存在两个评分层级：

步骤级（Step-level）评分能告诉你调用链在何处中断，这正是调试或开展针对性微调时所需的信息；而端到端（E2E）评分则将第一步的失败与第九步的失败一律归结为相同的“任务失败”。E2E 是用户实际体验到的指标，正因如此，大多数生产环境评估都以其作为发布门槛，同时保留底层的步骤级追踪以供调试。

这两个分数是对同一个对象的两种解读：即轨迹（trace）。轨迹是一次尝试的有序日志，包括：用户消息、每个步骤，以及当尝试终止时的环境状态。过程评分对这些行记录进行打分，而 E2E 评分则对最终状态进行打分。

工具调用基准测试按顺序对三项内容进行评分：决定是否使用工具、选择正确的工具，以及填充其参数。模型在可以直接回答时去调用工具，与遗漏本该调用的工具一样，都属于失败。成本和延迟则附加在最上层，由调用的冗长度和运行时间决定。

每一次运行都按照固定的层级自下而上汇总：基准测试（Benchmark）→ 试验（Trial）→ 任务（Task）→ 轮次（Turn）→ 步骤（Step）：

一个步骤通常是一次工具调用，其之上的所有评分均从这些步骤汇总而来。值得跟踪的指标主要集中在三个维度：准确性、冗长度、成本（参见下方表 1）。

指标的搭配非常关键：缺乏一致性的成功率只是对随机系统的一次点估计（一个先达到 90% 然后降至 74% 的模型，比稳定保持 84% 的模型更不可靠）；而缺少参数准确性的工具调用精确度，则会掩盖槽位填充层面的失败。

在同一任务中，步骤数量往往是不同模型之间差异最大的维度——例如四步对比十五步——不过在类似 Terminal-Bench 2.0 的套件中，每轮的步骤数也会有所不同，因此哪个维度的波动最大取决于具体的基准测试。并行工具调用可以减少步骤数和延迟，但不会减少调用次数：一个触发了四个工具的一步轮次，依然发出了四次调用。评估时应按顺序向上汇总，切勿简单地平均步骤数并将其作为基准测试得分。

两个基准测试可能都声称在测试工具调用，却得出不可比的数据。以下三个维度解释了其中大部分的差距：

数据污染如今已不再局限于训练数据泄漏，而是延伸至实时变体：具备网络搜索功能的 Agent 在评估期间检索答案，以及 Hugging Face 上的数据集迅速被重新抓取并纳入预训练语料库。私有领域评估通过无法被抓取来解决这一问题。

下方的表 2 是一个来自真实基准测试运行的公开轨迹，采用了步骤级和 E2E 评分，其中由测试套件而非人为编造的工单来提供工具、用户和完成标准。

查看输出的结果时，重点关注最后 5 个要点：E2E 检查、E2E 得分、步骤级得分、工具调用精确度以及参数准确性。E2E 检查表明其试图修复的缺陷相关测试均已通过，这意味着在当前情况下 E2E 得分为 1（is_resolved: true）。下一个指标是步骤级得分，它显示模型采取的步骤中有多少是真正必要的。查看上表中的得分，步骤级为 3/4，原因是本例中其中一个步骤是多余的——尤其是第 2 步。在这种情况下，它直接影响了工具调用精确度，由于这一轻微失误，该项得分同样为 3/4。在此轨迹中，我们的最终指标参数准确性显示所有参数均正确填充，没有格式错误的参数。

“调用工具”与“完成任务”之间的界限已不复存在：大多数衡量通用能力的基准测试现在也同时衡量工具使用，因为在任何可行的部署中，模型都不会在缺乏工具的情况下运行。剥夺工具访问权限的基准测试，衡量的是一种根本不会实际发布的无效能力。

并非每个基准测试都体现了这一点。HumanEval 针对单元测试运行生成的 Python 代码，提供了可执行的验证，但没有工具调用，也没有可供操作的环境。SWE-bench 则是这种转变变得清晰的地方：解决一个真实的 GitHub issue 意味着需要浏览代码库、编写补丁并使测试套件通过——这涉及按顺序进行的读取文件、搜索和编辑调用。得分衡量的是最终结果，但底层的轨迹完全由工具调用组成。因此，在许多情况下，你为了评估通用能力而运行的基准测试，实际上已经涵盖了工具使用。这就重新构成了真正重要的问题：

学术基准测试从抽象层面衡量模型的能力上限。企业级基准测试回答的则是更具体、更有用的问题：它能否胜任我的工作——在你的策略约束下，针对你的 API，执行你的任务？基准测试越接近生产实际，其得分在你的决策中所占的比重就应该越大。

阅读 NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 发布的测试套件时，应从任务完成度和完成耗时的角度切入，而非孤立的调用准确性。Banking 评估的是多轮银行对话中的完成情况——这是大规模真实退款轨迹的体现，而非单次调用。GDPval-AA v2 基于实际工作产出评估真实的 Agent 表现，由 LLM 评审团进行成对评判，其 Elo 分数锚定在 1,000 位人类专家的基线之上——这种人工验证保证了裁判评分的可靠性。在 PinchBench 上，Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 达到了 86% 的准确率，同时在可比的准确度下完成 10,000 个任务的速度比 Qwen3.6 35B 快 30%——一个高效完成任务的模型，胜过那些虽然在单点准确率上得分更高但消耗了更多步骤和 Token 的模型。

公开得分是一个极好的参考信号，但它们不应被视作发布的唯一准入标准。使模型适配你的具体任务和应用场景始终至关重要。

在环境中验证执行后果，使用裁判来评估语言质量，并利用工具调用精确度与参数准确性找出调用链断裂的位置。

为了复现已公布的数据，Nemotron 提供了可复现性文档，涵盖了模型卡片评分背后的配置。您可以在 build.nvidia.com 上进行体验，从 Hugging Face 获取权重，或者遵循 NIM 指南操作。

在大语言模型（LLM）基准测试领域，工具调用是当今评估体系的基石。能够构建、解读并理解这些评估，对于针对您的具体使用场景做出明智决策至关重要。

通过订阅 NVIDIA 新闻，并在 LinkedIn、X、YouTube 以及 Discord 上的 Nemotron 频道关注 NVIDIA AI，随时掌握 NVIDIA Nemotron 的最新动态。

您可以在 Hugging Face 上获取开源的 Nemotron 模型，并在 build.nvidia.com 上访问一系列 NIM 微服务和开发者示例。

aiStories.title: OpenAI其AI解决超百个悬案后成立数学顾问组
aiStories.originalTitle: OpenAI forms math advisory group as its AI resolves more than 100 open problems
aiStories.snippet: The group won't be given leeway to slow down or redirect OpenAI's ongoing mathematical research.
aiStories.fullContent:
On Monday, OpenAI announced a new independent advisory group hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey. Called the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, the group is meant to give mathematicians more input into the company’s math-oriented research.

“This group will serve as a bridge to the mathematical community and broader public, giving mathematicians a voice in how we move forward,” the post reads.

The announcement comes after the abrupt publication of a solution to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem. As part of the announcement of the new group, OpenAI also claims that the same internal model has resolved more than 100 additional open problems across most areas of mathematics.

Many prominent mathematicians have taken issue with the frenzied pace of those results. Earlier this month, 25 Fields Medal-winning mathematicians signed an open letter arguing that AI labs are threatening their intellectual work as they seek to one-up each other with solutions to famous math problems.

True to its name, OpenAI’s new group will mostly serve in an advisory capacity, assessing the significance of new results and coordinating their release. While members won’t be paid, they can offer unsolicited advice, go public with their views, and control their own membership, giving them a measure of independence from the company.

However, the group won’t be given leeway to slow down or redirect OpenAI’s ongoing mathematical research. As the blog post puts it, “the group will not be responsible for advising us on how to pace our internal progress on mathematics.”

The Institute for Advanced Study emphasized this point in its own announcement. “Although we will give advice, we do not have decision making power at any AI company, and the responsibility for the decisions made by any company will rest with that company,” said the institute in a press release.

Nine prominent mathematicians have been named as initial members of the group. Notably, only one of the members — IAS’s Camillo De Lellis — also signed the Fields Medalists’ letter.

周一，OpenAI宣布成立一个新的独立顾问组，设在新泽西州普林斯顿的高等研究院（IAS）。该团队名为“数学与人工智能顾问组”（Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence），旨在让数学家在OpenAI偏数学方向的研究中拥有更多发言权。

博文中写道：“该小组将充当通往数学界以及更广泛公众的桥梁，让数学家在我们如何前行方面拥有发声权。”

该公告发布前不久，纳维-斯托克斯千禧年大奖难题（Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem）的解答被仓促公开发表。作为公布新顾问组的一部分，OpenAI还声称同一个内部模型已经解决了数学绝大多数领域的另外100多个悬而未决的问题。

许多知名数学家对这些成果出炉时令人眼花缭乱的疯狂速度提出了异议。本月早些时候，25位菲尔兹奖得主签署了一封公开信，指出各家AI实验室在争先恐后地尝试用解答著名数学难题互相压制对方的过程中，正在对数学家的智力工作构成威胁。

名副其实的是，OpenAI的新顾问组主要扮演咨询角色，负责评估新成果的重大意义并协调其发布。尽管成员不领取报酬，但他们可以主动提供建议、公开发表自己的观点，并自主管理自身成员资格，这使他们对该公司保留了一定程度的独立性。

然而，该小组将无权减缓或改变OpenAI正在进行的数学研究的方向。正如博文所述：“该小组将不负责就如何掌控我们内部数学研发进度的节奏向我们提供建议。”

高等研究院在其官方公告中强调了这一点。该机构在一份新闻稿中表示：“尽管我们将提供建议，但我们在任何AI公司都不拥有决策权，任何公司所做决策的责任将完全由该公司自行承担。”

九位著名数学家被任命为该小组的初始成员。值得注意的是，这些成员中只有一位——IAS的卡米洛·德莱利斯（Camillo De Lellis）——此前也在菲尔兹奖得主的公开信上签了名。

trendStories.title: 我说“不”，苹果却说“要”
trendStories.originalTitle: I said no and Apple said yes
trendStories.fullContent:
Tuesday 22 Sept 2026 Play Synthesised Audio

The nice thing about keeping a blog is that I can say at precisely 9:51am, Wednesday 5th February 2025, I discovered that macOS 15.3 had enabled a feature that was phoning home every 15 minutes with personal data. And that I said “no” and turned it off.

At the time Apple were generous enough to provide a setting to disable this feature.

macOS 15 Apple Intelligence setting.

Although they hid the second part deeper, because why should saying “no” be easy?

macOS 15 Apple Intelligence privacy setting.

Last week I succumbed to Apple’s harassment and upgraded macOS 15 to 27. I only skipped one major version, Apple skipped 10!

And today I discovered that Apple had removed the “no” switch.

The “AI” industry has many flaws, the word “consent” being seemingly missing from training data and company handbooks is one of them. AI bros do not take “no” for an answer. When Apple advertised their deepfake feature back in June it became obvious Apple does not “think different.”

Digging through macOS 27 settings I turned off Siri (again). Of course, multiple unkillable Siri processes remain, stealing memory and writing data. For what purpose? Who knows. Note that they removed “Apple Intelligence” from this control.

macOS 27 Siri setting.

All of this garbage was enabled after upgrading to macOS 27 despite me having “Apple Intelligence & Siri” turned off already. That was a rather explicit “no”, no?

The icing on this cake is the 22.28 GB brick clogging my disk space.

macOS 27 Apple Intelligence accounting for 22.28 GB.

Apple is charging £500/TB on new MacBooks so that is what, £11 they’ve stolen from me?

But that’s a trivial cost compared to the consent problem. The AI industrial complex does not do consent. You will use it. You cannot look away, it will be stuffed down your throat and if you say “no” they’ll cut out your tongue.

The AI industry is vile. My AI policy tried to list my concerns but it’s hopelessly outdated. I can’t keep up. Here’s just three of many headlines I collected this month:

The list is endless. There is no limit to the human toll to keep this bubble inflated.

Call me a radical but I’ve chosen not to kowtow to billionaires. Do you want another Epstein list? Because this is how you create another Epstein list. Fund a generation of psychopaths building on a foundation of non-consent and privacy invasion. Fantastic idea!

AI bros keep telling me “just turn it off” and when I do they remove the choice.

All opinions are my own and not those of a large language model. Everything I write is one hundred percent human. Because I care!

I founded Valley Fold to help you, so let’s make your website happen. Whether you have requirements scoped or you’re lost for ideas, we can work with you at any stage.
trendStories.fullTranslation:
2026年9月22日，星期二 播放合成音频

写博客的一大好处在于，我可以准确记录下：2025年2月5日星期三上午9点51分，我发现macOS 15.3启用了一项每15分钟就会将个人数据传回服务器的功能。当时我说“不”，并把它关掉了。

那时苹果还算慷慨，提供了一个可以禁用该功能的设置项。

macOS 15 Apple Intelligence设置。

尽管他们把第二部分藏得更深——毕竟，说“不”怎么能那么容易呢？

macOS 15 Apple Intelligence隐私设置。

上周，我向苹果不断的骚扰妥协，将macOS 15升级到了27。我只跳过了一个大版本，苹果却直接跳过了10个！

而今天我发现，苹果已经把那个说“不”的开关给移除了。

“AI”行业存在诸多缺陷，训练数据和公司手册中似乎彻底缺失了“知情同意”（consent）这个词，便是其中之一。AI狂热者绝不接受拒绝。当苹果在6月份大肆宣传其深度伪造（deepfake）功能时，很显然苹果早已不再“非同凡想”（Think Different）。

翻遍macOS 27的设置，我（再次）关掉了Siri。当然，后台依然残留着多个无法杀死的Siri进程，占用着内存并不停写入数据。究竟出于什么目的？天晓得。注意，他们已经从这个控制项中移除了“Apple Intelligence”。

macOS 27 Siri设置。

尽管我此前已经关闭了“Apple Intelligence与Siri”，但在升级到macOS 27后，所有这些垃圾功能全被自动启用了。那明明是一个相当明确的拒绝，不是吗？

更糟糕的是，还有一个重达22.28 GB的“大砖头”死死霸占着我的磁盘空间。

macOS 27 Apple Intelligence占用了22.28 GB。

苹果新款MacBook的存储扩容收费高达每TB 500英镑，这么算来，他们等于从我这里偷走了11英镑？

但与“知情同意”问题相比，这点金钱代价根本微不足道。AI复合体从来不管什么知情同意。你必须使用它。你避无可避，它会被硬塞进你的喉咙；如果你敢说“不”，他们就会割掉你的舌头。

AI行业令人作呕。我的AI政策曾试图列出我的担忧，但如今它已彻底过时。我根本跟不上。以下是我本月收集的众多新闻头条中的三则：

这样的名单无休无止。为了维持这个泡沫的膨胀，所付出的人力代价没有任何底线。

随便你们说我激进好了，但我选择不向亿万富翁们卑躬屈膝。你们想要另一份爱泼斯坦名单吗？因为这正是制造下一份爱泼斯坦名单的温床。资助一群建立在“违背意愿”和“侵犯隐私”基础上的精神变态者，真是绝妙的主意！

AI狂热者老是对我说“关掉它不就行了”，而当我真的去关时，他们却直接把选择权给剥夺了。

所有观点均代表我个人，而非出自大型语言模型。我写下的每一个字都百分之百出自人类之手。因为我在乎！

我创办Valley Fold是为了帮助大家，让我们一起把你的网站做起来吧。无论你已经有了明确的需求范围，还是完全毫无头绪，我们都能在任何阶段与你展开合作。

系统资源的合理性：博主认为占用22GB空间和后台残留进程等于“偷窃资源”和流氓软件行径；厂商和支持者通常认为端侧大模型必须依赖本地权重和系统级守护进程。
blindSpots: 缺乏严谨的技术抓包与逆向证据，未能技术性证实系统每15分钟究竟回传了何种数据，亦未区分诊断日志、遥测数据与个人敏感数据。
将系统架构上的本地守护进程（Daemon）直接定性为“偷窃内存与写入数据的不可杀进程”，缺乏对现代操作系统后台服务机制的技术性客观评估。
文章包含大量高度情绪化甚至极端化的道德指控（如将AI行业类比爱泼斯坦名单、指责从业者为精神变态等），存在个人偏见与博文末尾商业推广（Valley Fold）的混合表达。

trendStories.title: 廉价易用的即用即弃式 VPN 服务器
trendStories.originalTitle: Cheap and easy throwaway VPN server
trendStories.fullContent:
In my previous blog post I mention I use to travel far and frequently and describe the gear I take with me to make it a more pleasant experience. Unfortunately not every place I visit offers the same kind and levels of freedoms I got used to growing up in a liberal democracy 🇪🇺.

To be completely honest, that by itself doesn’t usually limit my perceived freedoms much1, unrestricted internet access though might not always be possible without some kind of workaround and in this article I’m going to show you the ones I usually put in place to circumvent such restrictions.

By default I ignore the DNS resolvers offered by e.g. DHCP and use one of the freely available wildly known, usually Cloudflare’s. Setting one up in my minirouter2 means that’s going to be transparent for every other device connecting to my private LAN. Some provider allows for extra privacy like DNS over TLS and I recommend to turn it on because it generally comes with no perceivable extra latency, so why not?

This simple change by itself doesn’t help against filtered IP blocks or ports but it’s already useful in avoiding a series of other annoyances and, most importantly, it’s a fire-and-forget kind of configuration change that makes it a no brainer.

For years I’ve been a happy customer of Proton services and I can’t recommend them enough: they offer a simple and cost effective way to get rid of annoying ads-infested Google services while getting a big boost in privacy, there’s a free plan too so you can start for free and pay for the pro services only once you feel the need, like I did.

One problem I have with this is that it won’t let me choose the country on the exit side of the VPN. That’s reasonable for a free service but it might not help in solving the blocking/filtering problem if the exit country is also applying filters. More in general the quality of service might be degraded because of overloaded servers, so all in all is mostly hit and miss and I can’t rely on that as a stable solution.

There are more reasons why I want to be able to choose where the VPN exit point is located, for example some streaming platform might restrict or show different available content based on the geographical position of the source IP address, and so on.

I hear you: why not to pay for the pro ProtonVPN service too, or any of the many other VPN services out there? I could but it would be mostly a waste of money given that my need for a VPN connection is very spotty and never accounts for more than a few hours per month at worst.

What if I could just boot a pro VPN server on demand, pay only for the hours I use it and even choose in which region of the world it runs?

What I do when custom DNS and ProtonVPN aren’t helping is simple enough: I just spin up a WireGuard server with a single CLI command, connect my WireGuard clients to it as full tunnel, tear it down once I’m done with another CLI command.

Simple, fast, effective, and very cheap:

All I need to do is to copy (once) the printed WireGuard configuration into e.g. my Macbook’s WireGuard client and enable that to tunnel all the network traffic via the new VPN instance.

You can find the implementation in this repository hosted on my forge, it should be usable out of the box assuming you have OpenTofu5 installed and an AWS account to use.

The module doesn’t do much as you can see, I list the gist of it here for the ones who aren’t interested in the code:

Most of the default configuration values can be changed, refer to variables.tf for more details.

If for whatever reason you don’t want to use AWS, it should be relatively easy to (ask a coding agent to) modify the module to use your favorite provider instead, like Digital Ocean or else, and spin up the instance there instead.

The module has also a feature switch that lets me create a CNAME DNS record into my l3x.in zone that I host at Njalla but you can consider that as an implementation detail and use a different provider for that too, or simply ignore the extra DNS record and use the public EC2 DNS hostname directly; the repository is meant to be used as a blueprint more than a one-size-fits-all solution.

I’m sure many other valid solutions, like the ones offered by Tailscale, exist. I still prefer to bake my own and avoid creating yet another account / install other software on my workstation when the effort is relatively low.

For Tailscale in particular I find myself in this funny situation by which I admire their offering and at the same time I never feel like I need them because I can simply get away with just some WireGuard and iptables.

Most notably… where’s the fun going to be otherwise?

I hope you have found this helpful, as usual I’m looking forward to get your feedback, see /contact to get in touch with me.

Disclaimer: I don’t make use of any LLM help for writing my blog posts and this one is no exception.

Keep on rockin’ in the Free World Internet 🤘

applying for visas is still a pain though, especially here in South East Asia where I’m living right now ↩

see previous article about my travel setup ↩

I currently pay them US$83.76 for 24 months, so ~3.5USD/month ↩

or Terraform… but you should really use OpenTofu ↩

by default in the eu-south-1 (Italy) region ↩

you can cut this latency down sensibly if you are willing to ignore upgrading out-of-date OS packages, refer to https://forge.l3x.in/alex/aws-ec2-vpn/src/branch/master/cloud-init.yaml.tftpl for details ↩
trendStories.fullTranslation:
在我之前的博文中，我提到过我经常长途旅行，并介绍了随身携带的装备，正是它们让旅途体验更加愉快。遗憾的是，并非我到访的每个地方都能提供与我在自由民主国家🇪🇺成长过程中所习惯的同等种类和程度的自由。

坦白说，仅这一点本身通常并不会对我有感知的自由造成太大限制¹；然而，如果不采取某种变通方法，不受限制的互联网访问可能并非总能实现。在本文中，我将向大家展示我通常用来绕过此类限制的方案。

默认情况下，我会忽略 DHCP 等提供的 DNS 解析器，转而使用公开可用且广为人知的服务之一，通常是 Cloudflare 的。在我的便携微型路由器²中设置一个解析器，意味着对连接到我专用局域网的每台其他设备来说，这一过程都是透明无感的。有些提供商支持额外的隐私保护功能，例如 DNS over TLS，我建议开启它，因为通常它不会带来任何肉眼可见的额外延迟，何乐而不为呢？

单凭这一简单的改动并不能解决 IP 地址段或端口被过滤的问题，但它在避免一系列其他烦心事方面已经非常管用。最重要的是，这是一种一劳永逸式的配置更改，完全无需费神操作。

多年来，我一直是 Proton 服务的忠实用户，对其赞不绝口：他们提供了一种简单且极具成本效益的方式，既能摆脱令人厌烦且充斥广告的谷歌服务，又能大幅提升隐私安全性。他们还提供免费套餐，因此你可以免费起步，等到真正觉得有需要时再升级购买专业服务，就像我当时那样。

我对该服务唯一不满的一点在于：它不允许我自由选择 VPN 出口端的国家。对于一项免费服务来说这合情合理，但如果出口端国家本身也在实施网络过滤，这可能就无法解决屏蔽/过滤的问题了。更普遍的情况是，由于服务器过载，服务质量可能会有所下降，因此总体而言好坏全碰运气，我无法将其视作一种稳定的解决方案。

我想自主选择 VPN 出口节点所在位置的原因还不止于此，例如，某些流媒体平台可能会根据源 IP 地址的地理位置来限制内容或展示不同的可用内容，诸如此类。

我明白你想问什么：为什么不顺便购买 ProtonVPN 的付费专业版，或者市面上其他众多的 VPN 服务呢？我确实可以买，但鉴于我对 VPN 连接的需求非常零散，最极端情况下一个月加起来也用不上几个小时，买它基本上纯属浪费钱。

如果我能按需随时启动一台专业级 VPN 服务器，只需为使用的具体时长付费，甚至还能自主选择它在世界哪个地区运行，岂不美哉？

当自定义 DNS 和 ProtonVPN 都派不上用场时，我的做法其实很简单：只需运行一条 CLI 命令即可快速启动一台 WireGuard 服务器，将我的 WireGuard 客户端以全隧道模式连接到它，使用完毕后再运行另一条 CLI 命令将其销毁。

简单、迅速、高效且极其便宜：

我所需做的就是将打印出的 WireGuard 配置（一次性）复制到例如我的 MacBook 的 WireGuard 客户端中，并启用它，以便将所有网络流量通过这台全新的 VPN 实例进行隧道传输。

你可以在我代码托管平台上托管的这个代码仓库中找到具体实现。假定你已经安装了 OpenTofu⁵ 并且拥有可用的 AWS 账号，那么它应该可以开箱即用。

正如你所见，该模块并没有做太多复杂的事，在此我为那些对代码不感兴趣的人列出其核心要点：

大多数默认配置值都可以更改，详情请参考 variables.tf。

如果出于某种原因你不想使用 AWS，那么（让编程 AI 助手来）修改该模块以使用你喜欢的其他提供商（如 Digital Ocean 等）并改在那里启动实例，应该相对容易。

该模块还有一个功能开关，允许我在我托管于 Njalla 的 l3x.in 区域中创建一条 CNAME DNS 解析记录，但你可以将其视作一个实现细节，并在该环节使用其他提供商，或者直接忽略这条额外的 DNS 记录而直接使用 EC2 的公开 DNS 主机名；该代码仓库更倾向于用作蓝图参考，而非放之四海皆准的现成解决方案。

我确信存在许多其他切实可行的方案，比如 Tailscale 提供的方案。但我仍然更倾向于自己动手搭建，并且在所需精力相对较低的情况下，避免为了使用某项服务再去创建一个账号或在我的工作站上安装多余的软件。

特别是对于 Tailscale，我发现自己处于这样一种微妙的处境：我欣赏他们提供的产品，但与此同时我从未觉得非用他们不可，因为我只需借助少许 WireGuard 和 iptables 就能轻松搞定。

最值得一提的是……要是不这么折腾，乐趣又何在呢？

希望这篇文章对你有所帮助，与往常一样，我非常期待收到你的反馈，可通过 /contact 与我取得联系。

trendStories.title: 要闻：Git 2.56 版本包含 700 多个非合并提交
trendStories.fullContent:
The Git 2.56 release contains something over 700 non-merge commits; it brings a number of nice improvements, but will not fundamentally change the Git experience for most users. One feature that offers some potential in that regard is the addition of the drop subcommand to the (still experimental) git history toolbox:

This command will cause the identified commit to be removed from the history of the current branch, replaying all commits that were added after it. It offers an easier way of removing an offending commit. Unfortunately, it still refuses to work if the history contains merge commits, making it unusable for many (or most) repositories.

The git status command will now suggest a git pull command to update a branch that is behind the branch it tracks. It still, though, will say that a branch is "up to date" even if it lags behind an (unfetched) remote tracking branch.

The git refs command exists to manipulate references at a low level; in 2.56, it has gained a number of new subcommands. Those commands, create, delete, update, and rename, perhaps surprisingly for Git, do exactly what their names suggest they would.

There are a number of minor usability tweaks. The new --delete-merged option to git branch will remove local branches that have been merged into their remote tracking branches. An attempt to delete a branch with git branch -d will fail, with a useful message, if that branch is being used for bisection. Attempts to lock the configuration file will be retried on failures, avoiding annoyance when multiple commands try to modify the file at once. git add has a new --resolved option that only adds files with merge conflicts that have been resolved.

Beyond that, there is the usual long list of bug fixes, refactorings, and performance improvements. All told, 2.56 looks like a solid release, but it also shows the signs of a project that is holding back much of its more significant work for the future. That leads to the question of what comes next.

In early September, Git maintainer Junio Hamano asked the community what the next release should be. Would it be best to put out the 3.0 release that the community has been working toward for some time, finishing the year on a high note? Or, instead, is there a need for one or more 2.x releases still before the 3.0 release can happen?

This is an important question, because 3.0 will contain a number of compatibility breaks that may make some users pause before upgrading. Of those, perhaps the most significant is the switch to using the SHA-256 hash function by default, rather than the SHA-1 hash that Git has used since the beginning. SHA-1 has long been deemed to be weak, which is worrisome for applications like Git. Hashes are used to identify every object (files, directory trees, commits) in the Git repository, and are used to verify the chain of commits leading to any given point. If SHA-1 can be broken, it can conceivably be used to modify the history of a repository in ways that are difficult or impossible to detect.

Git has long included defenses against the known SHA-1 attacks, and few people appear to be seriously worried about the potential for compromised repositories now. Still, it makes a lot of sense to move to a more secure hash function.

Non-experimental support for SHA-256 has existed in Git since the 2.42 release in 2023, though some of the glue for interoperating with older repositories has taken longer. The biggest concern that has kept the Git developers from moving to SHA-256 by default for some time now has been support (or the lack thereof) at the major forge sites. GitLab has had support since 2024, and Forgejo has support as well. The elephant that is still missing from this room, though, is GitHub; releasing a version of Git that creates GitHub-incompatible repositories is a worrisome prospect. It still is not clear when GitHub might add that support, but it is notable that brian m. carlson, a GitHub employee and a key developer behind the SHA-256 transition, responded to Hamano's question by saying that news on that topic was coming, and that that having the next release be 3.0 might be the best choice.

That said, carlson has posted one other change that he would like to see added before 3.0 comes out. While Git has always managed hexadecimal numbers (specifically, object IDs) as lower-case strings, it has also accepted upper-case IDs. That leads to situations where two seemingly different IDs (f00f00 and F00F00, say) are actually the same. Seemingly, bugs and security vulnerabilities have arisen from this ambiguity. So carlson wants to change Git's behavior to only accept IDs in lower case. That is a change that, seemingly, should not cause problems for too many users, but there is almost certainly somebody somewhere who relies on that behavior.

Another significant change that has been waiting for the 3.0 release is the switch to the "reftable" mechanism. A reference (more commonly "ref") in Git is an association between a name and an object in the repository; branches, tags, and remotes are all refs, for example. Git currently (by default) stores each ref as a file under .git/refs/ in the repository. If a repository contains a branch called foo, there will be a file, .git/refs/heads/foo, containing the ID of the commit at the head of that branch. There is also a mechanism to pull all of these refs together into a packed-refs file, which increases performance — to a point.

This mechanism works, but becomes increasingly inefficient as the number of refs grows. In some projects, the number of refs does indeed grow. According to the project's reftable documentation, the Android repository contains over 800,000 refs. At that scale, looking up refs, or determining whether any refs pointing to a specific commit exist, can be an expensive operation. Slowing down development can be a yellow-card-level annoyance, leading to a desire to do something about the refs.

The Git 2.45 release added reftables as a more efficient way of storing refs. It is a binary file optimized for both space efficiency and quick access. Since then, it has been possible to create a repository that uses a reftable rather than the old file-based mechanism, but that has never been the default. Switching to reftable should have no visible consequences (other than better performance) for users of Git itself, but it can be a problem for users of other software packages that access Git repositories. In his email, carlson mentioned libgit2 as a potential concern.

As it turns out, libgit2 will not be a blocker here; Patrick Steinhardt let it be known that he has added reftable support to libgit2, and that SHA-256 support had been enabled by default in August. So libgit2 should be ready for the Git 3.0 transition.

Finally, as mentioned by carlson, there is the Rust question. The project has added some trial support for code written in Rust, but has hesitated to make Rust mandatory for the building of Git. That, too, is expected to change in the 3.0 release; after that, any platform that does not have a working Rust compiler will be unable to upgrade.

After listing these concerns, carlson suggested that they probably should not hold up the 3.0 release:

Similarly, I am not aware of anyone who is seriously undertaking Rust support for platforms that do not already support it, so I don't think that should be a blocker, either.

That led to his conclusion that, most likely, designating the next release as 3.0 would be the best choice.

What will actually happen has not, yet, been announced publicly; that is waiting for Hamano to make a decision. As he put it: "this is not a popularity contest, nor is it even a democracy". In the nearly two weeks since his query was posted, though, there has been no strong opposition to moving into the 3.x era and leaving some of Git's early design decisions behind (though, naturally, repositories using SHA-1 and lacking reftables will continue to be fully supported). If the 3.0 release does not happen in 2026, it seems certain to show up shortly thereafter.

Git 2.56 版本包含 700 多个非合并提交；它带来了许多不错的改进，但不会从根本上改变大多数用户的 Git 使用体验。在这方面颇具潜力的一项特性，是为（仍处于实验阶段的）git history 工具箱新增了 drop 子命令：

该命令将从当前分支的历史记录中移除指定的提交，并重新应用其后添加的所有提交。它为移除有问题的提交提供了一种更简便的方法。遗憾的是，如果历史记录中包含合并提交，该命令仍会拒绝工作，这导致它在许多（或大多数）代码仓库中无法使用。

git status 命令现在会建议运行 git pull 命令，以更新落后于其跟踪分支的本地分支。不过，即使分支落后于（尚未抓取的）远程跟踪分支，它仍然会提示该分支“已是最新”（up to date）。

git refs 命令用于在底层操作引用；在 2.56 版本中，它获得了若干新的子命令。这些子命令包括 create、delete、update 和 rename，对于 Git 来说可能有些出人意料——它们的功能完全正如其字面意思所示。

此外还有许多易用性方面的微调。git branch 新增的 --delete-merged 选项将移除已合并到对应远程跟踪分支的本地分支。如果某个分支正在用于二分查找（bisect），使用 git branch -d 尝试删除该分支将会失败，并给出有用的提示信息。锁定配置文件的尝试在失败时将进行重试，避免了多个命令同时尝试修改该文件时带来的困扰。git add 新增了 --resolved 选项，该选项仅暂存已解决合并冲突的文件。

除此之外，照例还有大量的错误修复、代码重构和性能提升。总的来说，2.56 看起来是一个稳健的版本，但它也显露出该项目正在为未来蓄力的迹象，将许多更重大的工作留待后续推出。这就引出了下一个问题：接下来会是什么？

9 月初，Git 维护者滨野纯（Junio Hamano）询问社区，下一个版本应该定为什么。是将社区一段时间以来一直在推进的 3.0 版本发布出来，为这一年画上圆满的句号？还是在 3.0 发布之前，仍需要再推出一个或多个 2.x 版本？

这是一个重要的问题，因为 3.0 将包含若干不向后兼容的重大改动，可能会让一些用户在升级前有所犹豫。其中，最显著的改动或许是将默认哈希函数切换为 SHA-256，而非 Git 从一开始就使用的 SHA-1 哈希。SHA-1 长期以来一直被认为安全性薄弱，这对于像 Git 这样的应用程序来说令人担忧。在 Git 仓库中，哈希值用于标识每一个对象（文件、目录树、提交），并用于验证导向任何特定节点的提交链。如果 SHA-1 能被攻破，理论上就可能被用来以难以察觉甚至无法察觉的方式篡改仓库历史。

Git 很早以前就已经包含了针对已知 SHA-1 攻击的防御措施，目前似乎很少有人严重担心仓库被篡改的可能性。尽管如此，转向更安全的哈希函数仍然十分必要。

自 2023 年发布的 2.42 版本起，Git 就已经提供了非实验性的 SHA-256 支持，不过用于与旧仓库互操作的某些粘合层耗费了更长时间。一段时间以来，阻碍 Git 开发者将 SHA-256 设为默认的最大顾虑在于各大代码托管平台的支持（或缺乏支持）。GitLab 自 2024 年起就已提供支持，Forgejo 也同样支持。然而，房间里那头依然缺席的大象是 GitHub；发布一个会创建与 GitHub 不兼容仓库的 Git 版本，是一个令人担忧的前景。目前仍不清楚 GitHub 何时会加入该支持，但值得注意的是，GitHub 员工兼 SHA-256 迁移背后的核心开发者 brian m. carlson 在回复滨野纯的问题时表示，关于该主题的消息即将公布，将下一个版本定为 3.0 可能是最佳选择。

话虽如此，carlson 还提出了另一项他希望在 3.0 发布前加入的改动。尽管 Git 一直将十六进制数（具体指对象 ID）作为小写字符串管理，但它也接受大写形式的 ID。这导致了两个表面上看起来不同（例如 f00f00 和 F00F00）的 ID 实际上是相同的情况。由于这种二义性，似乎已经引发了若干缺陷和安全漏洞。因此，carlson 希望更改 Git 的行为，使其仅接受小写 ID。这一改动按理说应该不会影响太多用户，但几乎可以肯定，在某些地方确实有人依赖于这种行为。

等待 3.0 版本的另一项重大改动是切换到“reftable”机制。Git 中的引用（通常简称为“ref”）是名称与仓库中对象之间的关联；例如分支、标签和远程跟踪分支都是引用。目前，Git（默认情况下）将每个引用作为文件存储在仓库的 .git/refs/ 目录下。如果仓库包含一个名为 foo 的分支，就会有一个文件 .git/refs/heads/foo，其中包含该分支顶端提交的 ID。此外还有一种将所有这些引用合并到单个 packed-refs 文件的机制，这能在一定程度上提高性能。

这种机制行之有效，但随着引用数量的增加，其效率会变得越来越低。在某些项目中，引用数量确实非常庞大。根据该项目的 reftable 文档，Android 仓库包含超过 80 万个引用。在这种规模下，查找引用或确定是否存在指向特定提交的引用，可能会成为一项开销极大的操作。拖慢开发节奏是一种令人十分烦躁的体验，进而促使人们希望对引用的存储方式进行改进。

Git 2.45 版本引入了 reftable，作为一种更高效的引用存储方式。它是一种针对空间效率和快速访问进行了优化的二进制文件。从那时起，用户就已经可以创建使用 reftable 而非旧有基于文件的机制的仓库，但这从未成为默认设置。切换到 reftable 对 Git 本身的用户来说应该没有任何显见的影响（除了性能提升），但对于使用访问 Git 仓库的其他软件包的用户来说，这可能会成为一个问题。carlson 在其邮件中提到了 libgit2 就是一个潜在的担忧点。

事实证明，libgit2 在这里不会成为阻碍；Patrick Steinhardt 透露，他已经为 libgit2 添加了 reftable 支持，并且 SHA-256 支持已在 8 月默认启用。因此，libgit2 应该已经为 Git 3.0 的过渡做好了准备。

最后，正如卡尔森（carlson）所提到的，还有 Rust 的问题。该项目已经为用 Rust 编写的代码增加了一些试验性支持，但一直对将 Rust 作为构建 Git 的强制要求持犹豫态度。预计这一点也将在 3.0 版本中发生改变；在此之后，任何没有可用 Rust 编译器的平台都将无法升级。
在列出这些担忧之后，carlson 提出，它们或许不应该阻碍 3.0 版本的发布：
“同样，我也没有听说有谁在认真致力于为那些尚不支持 Rust 的平台提供支持，因此我认为这也不应该成为阻碍。”
这让他得出结论：很可能将下一个版本命名为 3.0 会是最佳选择。
实际情况究竟如何，目前尚未公开宣布；这还在等待滨野（Hamano）做出决定。正如他所言：“这不是一场人气竞赛，甚至也不是民主投票。”不过，在他提出询问以来的近两周时间里，对于迈入 3.x 时代并摆脱 Git 早期的一些设计决策（当然，使用 SHA-1 且缺少 reftable 的代码仓库将自然会继续得到完全支持），并没有出现强烈的反对意见。如果 3.0 版本未能在 2026 年发布，那么几乎可以肯定它会在那之后不久亮相。
啊，GitHub 不支持 SHA-256 这个事实，简直让我想要去把所有的仓库都转换掉，这样它们就更难被镜像到 GitHub 了。😛

trendStories.title: 争鸣参数：关于函数形参与实参的思考
trendStories.fullContent:
Here’s some Rust code:

In programming language jargon, we call x and y parameters and 5 and 6 arguments.

Rust does not have many fancy features related to parameters and arguments. But other languages do. For example, here’s a function in Ruby, another language I’ve written a ton of:

I used to love Ruby, and now I love Rust. And to be honest, redirect_to and friends are a huge reason why I am so against Rust gaining these sorts of fancy features: they can be really concise, and beautiful to a certain kind of eye, but it also makes it really, really hard to know what all you can do with a function. You pretty much have to hope that someone has written good documentation, and while Rails’s documentation is pretty good, not every library is going to have it.

To be clear about it, there are several things bundled together here: flexible argument types, options hashes, defaults, and keyword-looking syntax. It’s that whole style of API that shaped my skepticism, not argument labels by themselves.

So, what exactly are all of these features?

The simplest one is named parameters. As you might guess, this means that we can explicitly use parameter names at the call site:

Named parameters are nice because they can give you more information at the call site, but also they can be more flexible. Some languages also let you supply named arguments in a different order:

The downside of named parameters is that they can get quite verbose:

I tried to not strawman this by showing an extreme example, but get can take 23 different keyword arguments, and so this could get quite, quite long.

Named arguments can be good when passing expressions, so we can understand something more at the call site. In the above, status_code=200 is much nicer than a bare 200, if you know HTTP well it’s kind of obvious what it is, but the additional clarity is nice. But it can be common to break truly complex examples down into variables that we end up forwarding to the function, and then it becomes verbose and redundant. As an example from inside FastAPI where get is invoked directly with all of those options:

We actually snuck in another two features into this example: how did we only pass five arguments into a function that has 23 parameters?

As the name implies, optional arguments is a feature where you can choose to not pass in an argument, and default arguments lets you set a default when an argument is not passed.

To go back to that example:

We only passed in five of the 22 possible arguments. If we had to pass all 22 every time, that would be extremely verbose. So by declaring defaults for some parameters, we can leave them off of the call site, and not pass arguments for them, and get the defaults instead. We saw this in the Ruby:

The = {} are defaults for options and response_options: they’re an empty hash map.

You’ll often find optional and default arguments come together: after all, if you don’t pass an argument in, what should the value of that parameter be? If your language has some sort of null value, that can be one solution, and it can feel like optional arguments without default arguments.

But you can truly get one without the other with our next feature, function overloading:

Languages that support function overloading allow you to define multiple functions with the same name, but different signatures. Which function gets invoked depends on which arguments you pass. This lets us truly have optional arguments without default arguments. In Java:

Here, if you pass in a timeout, you get the first function, and if you don’t, you get the second. Instead of null, the parameter just doesn’t exist at all.

This is a specific form of something called “function dispatch,” which basically means “hey when a function is invoked, what exactly gets called?” There are a lot of different ways to do this, and I don’t want this post to get into all of that right now, but there is a multitude of possibilities here: static vs dynamic, single vs multiple, predicate dispatch, pattern matching dispatch, prototype based dispatch… maybe I’ll write a post about that someday too.

So, what are the pros and cons here?

As I said above, Rust doesn’t support any of these three features right now. And they have been a persistent request from the community for years. Here is a 12 year old GitHub issue about this support, and it even includes something we didn’t talk about, “variable arity argument lists.”

That gets me to the first thing that I don’t like about these features: there are a lot of them. And they are all intertwined. As we mentioned before, if you have optional arguments, you probably want default arguments. If you have named parameters, do you want to support only named parameters, or do you want to support both? It’s so tempting to just support all of them, and then you’ve added a huge mountain of complexity.

In Rust right now, you have to write multiple functions with slightly different names:

For the simple cost of “write two different names for your functions,” you get to keep the rules very simple: there is one function definition, and you invoke it by name. Done. Would it be nice to be able to say all of these:

Sure, maybe. But the cost feels very, very high to me. If you’re used to these features, maybe it doesn’t seem that high, but I have a Ruby tattoo on my body. I’ve seen some shit. And so I’ve grown to enjoy Rust’s simplicity in this area. Yes, if you have a function with tons of parameters, you may need to write a builder instead, and that comes with its own form of verbosity:

But the language itself stays simple, and the rules are easy. For a language that’s already perceived as complex, this has always felt right to me. And that’s why I’ve pushed back against the various proposals to extend Rust in this way all of these years.

But recently, I changed my opinion on one of these features, and one alone, and I would consider it okay if Rust gained them. Maybe. Also, it’s important to note that I haven’t worked on Rust in years, and so my opinions are kind of irrelevant, but whatever: it’s my blog, this is what opinions are for.

I think Rust could be okay with named parameters, but not optional or default ones. And what changed my opinion is coding agents, actually. I’m sorry, maybe you’re sick of me talking about AI, but hear me out.

One of my beefs with named parameters, as mentioned above, is verbosity. But what you gain for that verbosity is clarity. I don’t think that verbosity and clarity are always the same thing; I like {} rather than do/end, and find it more readable, personally. But let’s take this function from the image crate:

This does really increase readability, no question about it. But for me, typing all of that out just isn’t really super worth the squeeze. But when Claude is gonna write it? I care a lot less. And the readability advantage for humans is even stronger for agents: the extra clarity of the text inline seems to (I haven’t run real evals on this yet…) be more helpful and use less tokens and calls when looking at the actual call site. If an agent were reading that named example above, it could tell that 10 is the x value without having to go look up the function signature itself. “What’s good for humans is true for agents” strikes again.

This is also why I’m still against optional arguments: they deliberately hide what is being passed in to the function, and obscure clarity at the call site. What’s nice about them is that you have to type less. But I’m not typing myself anymore. So the benefit just isn’t there, but the drawbacks are. This also doesn’t solve the verbosity side of passing foo=foo in our FastAPI example, it is still redundant. But one part of the downsides have been ameliorated.

Notably, all of this reasoning also applies to the builder pattern, and it’s why I try to use builders sparingly in Rust. It can emulate named arguments, which is good, but it can also emulate optional/default/variable arguments, which is bad. The juice is worth the squeeze sometimes, but not all the time, and probably not even the majority of the time.

So we’ve ameliorated the largest downside, but get to keep the largest upside. That seems good. But even if we like the feature, there are still lots of practical concerns with Rust specifically that make it not a slam-dunk to add them to the language.

Now, “is this feature good in the abstract” is very different from “should this feature” be implemented? There are a lot of open questions and drawbacks to implementing named parameters. A simple one is that you don’t get rid of all of those previous functions, with_capacity will exist forever. That’s a relatively minor downside to some of the harder problems.

First, strictly speaking Rust parameters aren’t names, they’re patterns. A name is a simple pattern, but you can get more complex:

This parameter doesn’t have a name, it’s a pattern that introduces two bindings. You could come up with some syntax that gives things external names vs internal names, but there’s that complexity revealing its head again.

What happens when functions become values? I can write this today:

What name do we use for f’s parameters? They can be named different things. Does this become an error? What names can you use when invoking f? Making this more complicated, Rust actually will accept this code right now:

The names in Callback are just documentation, as you can see they’re not required. Does this become an error? Do we require bar to change its names? The same goes for trait definitions, actually:

Is this an error? Is it okay?

Here’s another problem: evaluation order.

Right now, Rust always evaluates parameters from left to right at the call site. So if we use the named version:

If we keep left to right evaluation order according to the definition, but let you use named values in any order, suddenly some orders at the call site compile and some orders do not. Do we change evaluation order to do whatever compiles? That feels very dangerous and confusing.

Rust does let you do this with struct fields:

This is one reason why a lot of proposals for named arguments try to unify them with structs. As I said before, not insurmountable, just things that need to be sorted.

Another small thing is a compatibility hazard: if we start naming parameters, renaming them breaks callers. Is that okay? Could you introduce aliases to help with this? That’s more complexity…

These are just some of the problems that come up in the design space, and this post is getting long, so I’ll leave it at this for now. But proposals for doing this have to engage with all of this and more, which is why language design is difficult.

I like to think that I change my opinions over time as the world or my understanding of it changes. So I thought it might be interesting to share a way in which an opinion that I’ve held for over a decade has changed a bit lately. I’m still not sure if named parameters are right for Rust, but I’m at least somewhat open to the idea these days. We’ll see what the language team decides if anyone does decide to keep trying to push this forward. And people do, for example, I am writing this in part because I saw this post go by today. This post isn’t intended to be support or a rebuttal of it, I actually didn’t even read it yet, it’s just that I’ve been thinking about this a lot lately (while working on Rue) and seeing that go by pushed me to write some of the thoughts down. You should probably go check it out, as it’s an actual proposal in this space and this post is more of an exploration of the general idea and my own thoughts on it.

Here’s my post about this post on BlueSky:

Arguing about arguments steveklabnik.com/writing/argu...

Arguing about arguments

Here’s some Rust code: // define a function fn foo (x : i32 , y : i32 ) -> i32 { // body elided } // call it let z = foo ( 5 , 6 ); In programming language jargon, we call x and y parameters and 5 and 6 arguments . Rust does not have many fancy features related to parameters and…

在编程语言术语中，我们把 x 和 y 称为形参（parameters），把 5 和 6 称为实参（arguments）。
Rust 在形参和实参方面并没有太多花哨的特性。但其他语言有。例如，这里有一段 Ruby 函数，这也是我写过极多代码的另一门语言：
我曾经热爱 Ruby，而现在我热爱 Rust。说实话，redirect_to 及其同类特性，正是我如此反对 Rust 引入这类花哨特性的极大原因：它们确实可以非常简洁，并且在某些人眼里十分美观，但这也会让人们极难弄清楚一个函数到底能做些什么。你几乎只能寄希望于有人写了详尽的文档，尽管 Rails 的文档相当不错，但并不是每个库都能做到这一点。
明确地说，这里捆绑了几种特性：灵活的实参类型、选项哈希（options hashes）、默认值以及看似关键字参数的语法。正是这种整体的 API 风格塑造了我的怀疑态度，而不仅仅是实参标签本身。
那么，这些特性究竟都是些什么呢？
最简单的一个是具名参数（named parameters）。正如你可能猜到的那样，这意味着我们可以在调用处显式使用形参名称：
具名参数的好处在于它们可以在调用处为你提供更多信息，同时也更具灵活性。有些语言还允许你以不同的顺序传递具名实参：
具名参数的缺点在于它们可能会变得非常冗长：
我尽量不通过展示极端例子来树立稻草人谬误，但 get 函数可以接受 23 个不同的关键字实参，因此这可能会变得非常非常长。
在传递表达式时，具名实参会很有用，这样我们就能在调用处更好地理解某些信息。在上述示例中，status_code=200 显然比单纯的 200 好得多；如果你对 HTTP 很熟悉，它是什么显而易见，但额外的清晰度依然令人欣慰。然而，将真正复杂的调用拆解为变量再转发给函数是很常见的做法，此时它就变得冗长而多余了。举个来自 FastAPI 内部直接使用所有这些选项调用 get 的例子：
在这个例子中，我们实际上悄悄塞入了另外两个特性：我们怎么能只向一个拥有 23 个形参的函数传递五个实参呢？
顾名思义，可选实参（optional arguments）是一种允许你选择不传入某个实参的特性，而默认实参（default arguments）则允许你在没有传入实参时为其设定一个默认值。
回到刚才那个例子：
在 22 个可能的实参中，我们只传入了 5 个。如果每次都必须把全部 22 个传进去，那将极其冗长。因此，通过为某些形参声明默认值，我们可以在调用处省去它们，不必为它们传递实参，而是获取默认值。我们在 Ruby 中也见识过这一点：
其中的 = {} 就是 options 和 response_options 的默认值：它们是一个空哈希表（hash map）。
你通常会发现可选实参与默认实参是相伴相生的：毕竟，如果你不传入实参，那么该形参的值应该是什么呢？如果你的语言拥有某种 null 值，那可以作为一种解决方案，这感觉就像是没有默认实参的可选实参。
但是通过我们的下一个特性——函数重载（function overloading），你确实可以做到二者居其一：
支持函数重载的语言允许你定义多个同名但签名不同的函数。具体调用哪个函数取决于你传入的实参。这让我们真正实现了没有默认实参的可选实参。在 Java 中：
在这里，如果你传入 timeout，调用的就是第一个函数；如果不传，调用的就是第二个函数。形参根本就不存在，而不是值为 null。
这是一种被称为“函数分发”（function dispatch）的特定形式，其基本含义是“嘿，当一个函数被调用时，到底执行的是什么代码？”实现这一点有许多不同的方法，我现在不想在这篇文章中展开详述所有细节，但这里存在大量可能性：静态分发与动态分发、单分发与多分发、谓词分发、模式匹配分发、基于原型的分发……也许改天我也会就此写一篇文章。
那么，这些特性的优缺点究竟是什么？
正如我上面所说，Rust 目前不支持这三种特性中的任何一种。多年来，社区一直在不断呼吁支持这些特性。这里有一个关于此项支持长达 12 年之久的 GitHub issue，它甚至还包含了我们尚未讨论的内容——“可变参数列表”（variable arity argument lists）。
这就引出了我对这些特性不喜欢的首要原因：它们种类繁多，而且彼此交织在一起。正如我们之前提到的，如果你有了可选实参，你大概率会想要默认实参。如果你有了具名参数，你是想仅支持具名参数，还是想两者都支持？将它们全部支持的诱惑力太大了，而这样一来你就引入了一座巨大的复杂度大山。
在目前的 Rust 中，你必须编写多个名称略有不同的函数：
只需付出“为你的函数写两个不同的名字”这一简单代价，你就能让规则保持得极其简单：只存在一个函数定义，你通过名字来调用它。搞定。能够像下面这样调用难道不挺好的吗：
当然，也许吧。但对我而言，这其中的代价感觉非常非常高。如果你习惯了这些特性，也许会觉得代价没那么高，但我身上可是纹了 Ruby 纹身的，我见过太多混乱复杂的场面了。因此，我逐渐学会了欣赏 Rust 在这一领域的简洁性。是的，如果你的函数有大量形参，你可能需要转而编写一个构建器（builder），而这也会带来它自身形式的冗长：
但语言本身保持了简单，规则也容易理解。对于一门已经被认为很复杂的语言来说，这种做法一直让我觉得是正确的。这就是为什么多年来我一直反对各种试图以这种方式扩展 Rust 的提案。
但是最近，在这些特性中，我对其中某一个特性的看法发生了改变，仅仅是这一个特性，如果 Rust 引入它，我认为是可以接受的。也许吧。另外需要说明的是，我已经多年没有从事 Rust 的开发工作了，所以我的看法其实无关紧要，但无所谓了：这是我个人的博客，博客就是用来表达观点的。
我认为 Rust 引入具名参数是可以接受的，但不能包含可选参数或默认参数。实际上，改变我看法的是 AI 编码代理（coding agents）。很抱歉，也许你们已经厌烦了我谈论 AI，但请听我解释。
正如上面所提到的，我对具名参数的不满之一是冗长。但伴随这种冗长而来的，是清晰度。我认为冗长和清晰度并不总是同一回事；就个人而言，我更喜欢 {} 而不是 do/end，觉得前者更具可读性。但让我们来看看 image crate 中的这个函数：

这确实极大地提高了可读性，毫无疑问。但对我来说，把这一切全敲出来实在有些得不偿失。然而如果是 Claude 来写呢？我可就没那么介意了。而且对人类而言的可读性优势，在智能体（agent）身上体现得更加明显：行内文本额外的清晰度似乎在查看实际调用位置时更有帮助，并且消耗更少的 token 和调用次数（我尚未对此做过真正的评测……）。如果一个智能体在阅读上面那个命名参数的示例，它无需去查阅函数签名本身，就能知道 10 就是 x 的值。“对人类有益的同样对智能体成立”再次应验。

这也是为什么我依然反对可选参数：它们刻意隐藏了传递给函数的内容，并在调用点模糊了清晰度。它们的好处在于你可以少打些字。但我现在已经不再亲自打字了。因此收益荡然无存，而弊端却依然存在。这同样无法解决在我们的 FastAPI 示例中传递 foo=foo 的冗长问题，它依旧是冗余的。但部分弊端确实得到了缓解。

值得注意的是，所有这些推理同样适用于建造者模式（builder pattern），这也是我尽量在 Rust 中少用建造者的原因。它可以模拟命名参数，这很好；但它也可以模拟可选/默认/可变参数，这很糟糕。有时确实值得这么折腾，但并非总是如此，甚至大概率大部分时候都不值得。

所以，我们缓解了最大的弊端，却保留了最大的优势。这看起来不错。但即使我们喜欢这一特性，在 Rust 中具体实现时仍然存在许多实际考量，使其绝非能轻易顺理成章地加入到语言中。

现在，“这个特性在抽象层面上是否优秀”与“这个特性是否应该被实现”是截然不同的两码事。实现命名参数存在许多悬而未决的问题和弊端。一个简单的问题是，你无法摆脱以往所有的那些函数，with_capacity 将永远存在。与某些更棘手的问题相比，这只是一个相对较小的缺点。

首先，严格来说，Rust 的形参（parameters）不是名称，而是模式（patterns）。名称只是一种简单的模式，但你可以写得更复杂：

这个形参没有名称，它是一个引入了两个绑定的模式。你可以设计某种语法来区分外部名称和内部名称，但那种复杂性又会再次浮现。

当函数变成值时会发生什么？我今天可以这样写：

f 的参数我们该用什么名字？它们可以有不同的命名。这会导致报错吗？在调用 f 时你可以使用哪些名称？更复杂的是，Rust 目前实际上会接受这样的代码：

Callback 中的名称仅仅是文档说明，正如你所见，它们并不是必需的。这会导致报错吗？我们要强制 bar 更改其名称吗？实际上，trait 定义也是如此：

这是个错误吗？还是可以接受？

这里还有另一个问题：求值顺序（evaluation order）。

目前，Rust 在调用位置始终从左到右对实参求值。因此如果我们使用命名版本：

如果我们按照定义保持从左到右的求值顺序，但允许你在调用时以任意顺序使用具名值，突然之间，调用点的某些顺序可以通过编译，而某些顺序却无法编译。我们要为了让任何写法都能编译而改变求值顺序吗？这让人感觉非常危险且混乱。

Rust 确实允许你对结构体字段这样做：

这就是为什么许多关于命名实参的提案都试图将其与结构体统一起来的原因之一。正如我之前所说，这并非无法逾越，只是需要梳理解决的事情。

另一件小事是兼容性隐患：如果我们开始对形参进行命名，重命名形参就会破坏调用者的代码。这能被接受吗？你能引入别名来协助解决这个问题吗？那又会带来更多复杂性……

这些只是设计领域中出现的部分问题，由于这篇文章已经写得很长了，所以我就先谈到这里。但是相关的提案必须直面所有这些问题乃至更多挑战，这也是语言设计之所以困难的原因。

我常常认为，随着世界的变化或自己对世界认知的改变，我的观点也会随之改变。因此我认为，分享一下我持有了十多年的某个观点最近是如何发生些许转变的，可能会很有意思。我仍然不确定命名形参是否适合 Rust，但这些天我至少对这个想法抱有一定开放态度。如果有人决定继续推进这项工作，我们将静观语言团队的决定。确实有人在推进，例如，我写下本文的部分原因就是今天看到了那篇文章。本文并非旨在支持或反驳它，实际上我甚至还没有读过它，只是我最近在思考很多这方面的问题（在开发 Rue 时），看到那篇文章促使我写下了这些想法。你或许应该去读一读那篇文章，因为它是该领域中一个切实具体的提案，而本文更多是对通用构想及我个人思考的探讨。

trendStories.fullContent:
Women escaping abusive partners abroad could get new protections from legal analysis of Hague convention

British mothers who bring their children with them when returning to the UK after fleeing from domestic abuse abroad – which can lead to them being accused of abduction – could be given greater legal protection and support.

The government has agreed to examine how domestic abuse features in international child abduction cases, with a view to giving survivors of domestic abuse more help fighting partners’ demands that they return children to their home countries.

In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid . In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org .
trendStories.fullTranslation:
通过对《海牙公约》的法律分析，逃离海外虐待伴侣的女性或将获得新的保护。

英国母亲在逃离海外家庭暴力后携子女返回英国——这一行为可能导致她们被指控拐带儿童——未来有望获得更有力的法律保护与支持。

政府已同意审查国际拐带儿童案件中涉及家庭暴力的具体情形，旨在为家暴幸存者提供更多帮助，以应对伴侣要求将子女送回所在国的诉求。

在英国，可拨打全国反家暴求助热线 0808 2000 247，或访问“妇女援助组织”（Women’s Aid）。在美国，反家庭暴力热线为 1-800-799-SAFE (7233)。在澳大利亚，全国家庭暴力咨询服务热线为 1800 737 732。其他国际求助热线可通过 www.befrienders.org 查询。

trendStories.source: The Guardian Society (卫报社会与民生)
